domanda: Contoso runs a business-critical virtual machine named VM-ERP in a resource group named RG-Prod. Operations engineers must still be able to resize VM-ERP, attach data disks, and restart it, but no one in the organization - including subscription owners - may delete it. What should you configure?
opzione_d: An Azure Policy assignment that uses the deny effect, scoped to RG-Prod
spiegazione: Correct: a. A CanNotDelete lock (shown as 'Delete' in the portal) means authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete it. Because a management lock applies across all users and roles and overrides user permissions, even a subscription Owner cannot delete VM-ERP while the lock exists, yet resize, disk attach, and restart operations still succeed. Wrong: b. A ReadOnly lock means authorized users can read a resource but can't delete or update it - it is similar to restricting all users to the permissions of the Reader role, so it would block the required resize and disk-attach operations. Wrong: c. A ReadOnly lock on the resource group is inherited by every resource in it and is even more restrictive: a read-only lock on a resource group that contains a virtual machine prevents all users from starting or restarting that virtual machine, because those operations require a POST request. Wrong: d. The deny effect of Azure Policy evaluates create and update requests against resource properties; it is not the mechanism for blocking deletion. The effect designed to block delete calls is denyAction, whose only supported action name today is 'delete'. A management lock is the feature Microsoft documents for protecting resources from accidental deletion.

sotto_argomento: Apply and manage tags on resources
domanda: A resource group named RG-Finance is tagged with CostCenter = CC-4410 and Environment = Production. A colleague deploys a new storage account into RG-Finance by using a Bicep file that does not define any tags. No Azure Policy assignments exist in the subscription. You open the storage account in the Azure portal and view its Tags page. What do you see?
opzione_a: The storage account has CostCenter = CC-4410 and Environment = Production, inherited from RG-Finance.
opzione_b: The storage account has both tags, but they are displayed as read-only and cannot be changed on the storage account.
opzione_c: The storage account has no tags.
opzione_d: The storage account has no tags now, but inherits both tags automatically at the end of the next Azure Policy evaluation cycle.
spiegazione: Correct: c. Microsoft documents this explicitly: resources don't inherit the tags you apply to a resource group or a subscription. Tag inheritance is not a built-in behaviour of Azure Resource Manager, so a resource deployed with no tags has no tags, regardless of what its parent resource group carries. Wrong: a. This is the classic misconception. Tags on a resource group describe only the resource group object itself; they are never automatically copied down to the resources inside it. Wrong: b. There is no notion of an inherited, read-only tag on a child resource. Tags applied to a resource are always writable by anyone with tag write access on that resource. Wrong: d. Automatic tag inheritance only happens if you assign a tag policy such as 'Inherit a tag from the resource group', and even then the modify effect does not change resources that already exist during an evaluation cycle - it marks them non-compliant so they can be fixed with a remediation task. With no policy assigned, no evaluation cycle will ever add the tags.

domanda: A support engineer applies a Read-only lock to a storage account named stcontoso01. Shortly afterward, a line-of-business application that retrieves its connection string from the storage account's Access keys page starts to fail, and the engineer can no longer display the account keys in the Azure portal even though the engineer is an Owner of the subscription. What explains this behaviour?
opzione_a: A ReadOnly lock blocks all data plane requests to the storage account, so the keys can no longer be used.
opzione_b: The List Keys operation is handled by a POST request to the Azure Resource Manager API, and a ReadOnly lock blocks it.
opzione_c: Applying a ReadOnly lock automatically disables shared key authorization on the storage account.
opzione_d: Applying a ReadOnly lock automatically rotates both storage account keys, invalidating the cached connection string.
spiegazione: Correct: b. Microsoft documents that a read-only lock on a storage account prevents users from listing the account keys, because a POST request handles the Azure Storage List Keys operation, and locks prevent the POST method from sending data to the Azure Resource Manager API. The lock overrides any user permissions, so being an Owner does not help. Users who don't have the account keys need to use Microsoft Entra credentials to access blob or queue data. Wrong: a. Locks only apply to control plane Azure operations (requests to management.azure.com) and not to data plane operations. Clients that already hold a key or SAS can still read and write blob data; the lock does not protect the data itself. Wrong: c. A lock never changes a resource's configuration. Disabling shared key authorization is a separate storage account property (allowSharedKeyAccess) that an administrator must set explicitly - and a ReadOnly lock would in fact block that change. Wrong: d. Locks do not perform any action on the resource; key rotation is a deliberate administrative operation (and it is itself a control plane POST that the lock would block).
tags: resource locks,readonly lock,storage account,list keys,control plane

domanda: The governance team applies a Read-only lock at the scope of a resource group named RG-App1. RG-App1 contains a virtual machine named VM-App1, an App Service plan named ASP-App1, and a storage account named stapp101. All administrators hold the Owner role on the subscription. Which operation still succeeds while the lock is in place?
opzione_a: Starting VM-App1 after it has been stopped (deallocated)
opzione_b: Scaling up ASP-App1 to a higher pricing tier
opzione_c: Reading blob data from stapp101 by using a client application and an account key that was retrieved before the lock was applied
opzione_d: Moving VM-App1 from RG-App1 to a different resource group
spiegazione: Correct: c. Locks only apply to control plane Azure operations and not to data plane operations. A read-only or cannot-delete lock on a storage account doesn't protect its data from being read, modified, or deleted, so an application holding a valid account key continues to read blob data through the data plane endpoint (for example https://stapp101.blob.core.windows.net). Wrong: a. A read-only lock on a resource group that contains a virtual machine prevents all users from starting or restarting that virtual machine, because those operations require a POST method request. Wrong: b. A read-only lock on a resource group that contains an App Service plan prevents you from scaling up or out of the plan. Wrong: d. A read-only lock on a resource group prevents you from moving existing resources in or out of that resource group. (Note the asymmetry Microsoft calls out: you can move a resource that itself carries a read-only lock to another resource group - it is the lock on the resource group that blocks the move here.)
tags: resource locks,readonly lock,control plane,data plane,app service plan

domanda: A platform engineer named Diego is assigned the Contributor role at the scope of a subscription. When Diego tries to create a Delete lock on a resource group, the request fails with an authorization error. Diego must be able to create and remove management locks, but must not be granted the ability to create, modify, or delete the resources themselves. Which built-in role should you assign to Diego?
spiegazione: Correct: b. To create or delete management locks, you need access to Microsoft.Authorization/* or Microsoft.Authorization/locks/* actions, and Microsoft names Owner and User Access Administrator as the built-in roles that have the required access. User Access Administrator's Actions are */read, Microsoft.Authorization/*, and Microsoft.Support/* - it therefore grants the lock actions while granting no write access to resources, which satisfies the constraint. This also explains the failure: Contributor grants Actions '*' but carries the NotActions Microsoft.Authorization/*/Write and Microsoft.Authorization/*/Delete, so it cannot create or delete locks. Wrong: a. Owner does have the required access (Actions '*' with no NotActions), but it grants full access to manage all resources, which violates the requirement that Diego must not be able to create, modify, or delete resources. Wrong: c. Resource Policy Contributor covers Azure Policy definitions and assignments, not Microsoft.Authorization/locks. Wrong: d. Management Group Contributor lets you manage management groups; it does not grant the lock actions at subscription or resource group scope, and locks cannot be applied to management groups at all.

domanda: In a subscription named Sub-Prod, a CanNotDelete lock named lock-sub is applied at the subscription scope. A resource group in that subscription named RG-Data has a ReadOnly lock named lock-rg. RG-Data contains an Azure SQL logical server named srv-data01. An engineer who holds the Owner role on Sub-Prod attempts to add a server-level firewall rule to srv-data01 through the Azure portal. What is the result?
opzione_a: The operation succeeds, because the CanNotDelete lock at the subscription scope is applied first and takes precedence over locks at lower scopes.
opzione_b: The operation succeeds, because management locks restrict only users who are not assigned the Owner role.
opzione_c: The operation fails, because srv-data01 inherits the ReadOnly lock from RG-Data and the most restrictive lock in the inheritance chain takes precedence.
opzione_d: The operation fails, because a CanNotDelete lock at the subscription scope blocks every write operation in the subscription.
spiegazione: Correct: c. When you apply a lock at a parent scope, all resources within that scope inherit the same lock, and the most restrictive lock in the inheritance chain takes precedence. srv-data01 therefore inherits both CanNotDelete (from the subscription) and ReadOnly (from RG-Data); ReadOnly is the more restrictive, so authorized users can read the server but can't delete or update it. Creating a firewall rule is a control plane write, so it fails. Wrong: a. Precedence is not determined by scope order or by which lock is 'closest' - it is always the most restrictive lock that wins. Wrong: b. Unlike Azure RBAC, management locks apply a restriction across all users and roles; the lock overrides any user permissions, including Owner. Wrong: d. CanNotDelete means authorized users can read and modify the resource but can't delete it. It does not block write operations - the ReadOnly lock is what blocks this request.

sotto_argomento: Apply and manage tags on resources
domanda: You assign the Tag Contributor built-in role to a cost analyst named Ava at the scope of a subscription. Ava signs in to the Azure portal, opens the Tags page of a resource group, adds a tag, and selects Save - but the operation fails. Ava must be able to apply tags to resource groups and to individual resources in the subscription. Ava must not be able to create, modify, or delete the resources themselves, and you must follow the principle of least privilege. What should you do?
opzione_a: Assign Ava the Reader role at the subscription scope in addition to Tag Contributor.
opzione_b: Assign Ava the Contributor role at the subscription scope instead of Tag Contributor.
opzione_c: Remove the subscription-scoped assignment and assign Tag Contributor separately at each resource group scope.
opzione_d: Instruct Ava to apply the tags by using Azure PowerShell, the Azure CLI, or the REST API instead of the Azure portal.
spiegazione: Correct: d. This is a documented limitation of the role, not a misconfiguration. Tag Contributor grants write access to the Microsoft.Resources/tags resource type, which lets the holder tag any resource even without access to the resource itself. However, Microsoft states that this role can't apply tags to resources or resource groups through the Azure portal, although it can apply tags to subscriptions through the portal, and it supports all tag operations through Azure PowerShell and the REST API. Using a non-portal client is therefore the fix that keeps least privilege intact. Wrong: a. The failure is not caused by missing read access. Adding Reader grants only */read on the resources and does not change the portal's behaviour for tagging resources and resource groups. Wrong: b. Contributor does grant the required access to apply tags to any entity through the portal, because it grants write access to the resource itself - but it also grants full access to manage all resources, which breaks both stated requirements. Wrong: c. The portal limitation is a property of the Tag Contributor role, not of the scope at which it is assigned; re-assigning it lower in the hierarchy changes nothing.

sotto_argomento: Apply and manage tags on resources
domanda: Your organization is drafting a tagging standard for all Azure workloads and needs to document the platform constraints correctly. Which statements about Azure resource tags are true? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Each resource, resource group, and subscription can have a maximum of 50 tag name-value pairs.
opzione_b: A tag name is limited to 512 characters, except for storage accounts, where the tag name is limited to 128 characters.
opzione_c: Tag names are case-insensitive for operations, but tag values are case-sensitive.
opzione_d: Tags can be applied to management groups in the same way that they are applied to subscriptions.
opzione_e: A tag value is limited to 1,024 characters.
spiegazione: Correct: a. Microsoft documents that each resource, resource group, and subscription can have a maximum of 50 tag name-value pairs. If you need more, use a JSON string as a single tag value to pack multiple values under one tag name. Correct: b. The tag name has a limit of 512 characters and the tag value has a limit of 256 characters; for storage accounts, the tag name limit is 128 characters (the value limit stays 256). Correct: c. Tag names are case-insensitive for operations - an operation updates or retrieves a tag regardless of casing, although the resource provider might preserve the casing you supplied and you see that casing in cost reports. Tag values are case-sensitive. Wrong: d. You can apply tags to Azure resources, resource groups, and subscriptions but not to management groups. Wrong: e. 1,024 is not the tag value limit. The tag value has a limit of 256 characters. Also worth knowing for the standard: tag names can't contain the characters < > % & \ ? / and some services (Azure Automation, Azure CDN, Azure Public and Private DNS zones and A records, Log Analytics saved searches) support only 15 tags.

domanda: During a change freeze, your team applies a Read-only lock at the scope of a resource group named RG-Shared. RG-Shared contains a storage account, an App Service plan that hosts a web app, a network security group, and an Azure Automation account. You must warn the operations team about what will stop working. Which operations does the lock block? Select all that apply.
opzione_a: Listing the storage account's access keys from the Azure portal
opzione_b: Uploading a blob to an existing container by using a shared access signature that was issued before the freeze
opzione_c: Scaling up the App Service plan to a higher pricing tier
opzione_d: Viewing the security rules of the network security group in the Azure portal
opzione_e: Starting a runbook in the Automation account
spiegazione: Correct: a. A read-only lock on a storage account prevents users from listing the account keys, because the List Keys operation is handled by a POST request to Azure Resource Manager and locks prevent the POST method from sending data to the ARM API. Correct: c. A read-only lock on a resource group that contains an App Service plan prevents you from scaling up or out of the plan. Correct: e. A read-only lock on a resource group that contains an automation account prevents all runbooks from starting, because those operations require a POST method request. Wrong: b. Locks only apply to control plane Azure operations and not to data plane operations. A blob upload goes to the service endpoint rather than to management.azure.com, so the lock does not block it - a read-only or cannot-delete lock on a storage account doesn't protect the data in a blob, queue, table, or file. Wrong: d. ReadOnly means authorized users can read the resource; it is similar to restricting all authorized users to the permissions that the Reader role provides. Reading the NSG's rules is exactly what the lock still permits. (Note that a read-only lock on an NSG would block creation of the corresponding NSG flow log, which is a write.)
tags: resource locks,readonly lock,automation account,app service plan,post method,data plane

sotto_argomento: Apply and manage tags on resources
domanda: Contoso tags every resource group with a CostCenter tag. The finance team reports that Microsoft Cost Management shows no CostCenter value for several hundred virtual machines and managed disks that already exist inside those resource groups. You must ensure that every existing resource, and every resource created in the future, carries the CostCenter value of its parent resource group. Any CostCenter value already set on a resource must be overwritten with the resource group's value. You must minimize administrative effort. Select the appropriate option for each requirement.
opzione_a: Built-in policy definition to assign: [Require a tag on resources | Inherit a tag from the resource group | Append a tag and its value from the resource group]
opzione_b: Policy effect that this definition uses: [Append | Deny | Modify]
opzione_c: Prerequisite for the policy assignment: [A managed identity that is granted a role including tag write permissions | A Log Analytics workspace in each resource group | An Azure Automation account with a Run As account]
opzione_d: Action required to tag the resources that already exist: [Wait for the next policy evaluation cycle | Create a remediation task | Redeploy each resource from its ARM template]
risposta_corretta: Inherit a tag from the resource group,Modify,A managed identity that is granted a role including tag write permissions,Create a remediation task
spiegazione: Correct dropdown 1: 'Inherit a tag from the resource group'. Microsoft describes this built-in definition as: 'Adds or replaces the specified tag and value from the parent resource group when any resource is created or updated. Existing resources can be remediated by triggering a remediation task.' The addOrReplace behaviour matches the requirement to overwrite an existing value. 'Require a tag on resources' only enforces the existence of a tag with the deny effect and never applies a value. 'Append a tag and its value from the resource group' uses the append effect and 'Does not modify the tags of resources created before this policy was applied until those resources are changed', so it cannot fix the existing resources. Correct dropdown 2: 'Modify'. The 'Inherit a tag from the resource group' definition uses the modify effect, which adds, updates, or removes tags on a subscription or resource during creation or update, and supports remediating existing non-compliant resources. Correct dropdown 3: 'A managed identity that is granted a role including tag write permissions'. Policy assignments with effect set as Modify require a managed identity to do remediation; the identity can be system-assigned or user-assigned, and the role defined in roleDefinitionIds must include all operations granted to the Contributor or Tag Contributor role. A Log Analytics workspace and an Automation account are unrelated to Modify remediation. Correct dropdown 4: 'Create a remediation task'. When a policy definition using the modify effect is run as part of an evaluation cycle, it doesn't make changes to resources that already exist - it only marks them non-compliant so they can be remediated through a remediation task. Waiting therefore never tags them, and redeploying every resource is possible but is the opposite of minimizing administrative effort.
tags: tags,azure policy,modify effect,remediation task,managed identity,tag inheritance

domanda: A resource group named RG-Web contains a web app named app-web01 and the App Service plan that hosts it, named ASP-Web. A CanNotDelete lock named lock-web is applied to app-web01 only. No other management locks exist anywhere in the subscription. All administrators hold the Owner role on the subscription. Select the outcome of each operation.
opzione_a: An administrator deletes the RG-Web resource group: [Succeeds | Fails - the entire delete operation is blocked | Succeeds - every resource except app-web01 is deleted]
opzione_b: An administrator deletes a diagnostic setting that is applied to app-web01: [Succeeds | Fails - the extension resource inherits the lock from app-web01 | Succeeds - but only after the lock notes are cleared]
opzione_c: A developer deploys updated application code to app-web01: [Succeeds | Fails - the lock blocks all write operations | Fails - the lock blocks data plane requests]
opzione_d: An engineer scales up ASP-Web to a higher pricing tier: [Succeeds | Fails - ASP-Web inherits the lock from app-web01 | Fails - the lock blocks POST requests to the subscription]
risposta_corretta: Fails - the entire delete operation is blocked,Fails - the extension resource inherits the lock from app-web01,Succeeds,Succeeds
spiegazione: Correct dropdown 1: 'Fails - the entire delete operation is blocked'. Microsoft states that if you have a Delete lock on a resource and attempt to delete its resource group, the whole delete operation is blocked - even if the resource group and the other resources in it are unlocked - because a partial deletion isn't possible. Correct dropdown 2: 'Fails - the extension resource inherits the lock from app-web01'. Extension resources inherit locks from the resource to which they're applied, and Microsoft.Insights/diagnosticSettings is an extension resource type. Because the diagnostic setting's full resource ID is nested under app-web01's resource ID, the lock on app-web01 blocks the delete. Correct dropdown 3: 'Succeeds'. CanNotDelete means authorized users can read and modify a resource, but they can't delete it. Only ReadOnly blocks write operations, so a code deployment is unaffected. Correct dropdown 4: 'Succeeds'. Locks are inherited downward from a parent scope to the resources within it; ASP-Web is a sibling resource in the same resource group, not a child of app-web01, so it inherits nothing from lock-web. (Had the lock been a ReadOnly lock on RG-Web instead, this scale-up would have failed, because a read-only lock on a resource group that contains an App Service plan prevents scaling the plan up or out.)
tags: resource locks,cannotdelete,lock inheritance,extension resources,diagnostic settings,app service

domanda:
Your organization protects production workloads with management locks. A subscription named Sub-Prod sits under a management group named MG-Production and contains a resource group named RG-Core. RG-Core contains a storage account named stcore01. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true.

1. A CanNotDelete lock applied to RG-Core also prevents the deletion of resources that are added to RG-Core after the lock was created.
2. You can apply a ReadOnly lock to MG-Production to protect every subscription beneath it.
3. A CanNotDelete lock on stcore01 prevents a user from deleting a blob in stcore01 by using AzCopy with a valid account key.
opzione_a: A CanNotDelete lock applied to RG-Core also prevents the deletion of resources that are added to RG-Core after the lock was created.
opzione_b: You can apply a ReadOnly lock to MG-Production to protect every subscription beneath it.
opzione_c: A CanNotDelete lock on stcore01 prevents a user from deleting a blob in stcore01 by using AzCopy with a valid account key.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - Yes. When you apply a lock at a parent scope, all resources within that scope inherit the same lock, and Microsoft explicitly notes that even resources you add later inherit the same parent lock. Inheritance is evaluated at request time, not captured when the lock is created. Statement 2 - No. Microsoft states that you can't add a lock to management groups. Locks can be scoped to a subscription, a resource group, or an individual resource only. To protect every subscription under MG-Production you would have to place a lock on each subscription. Statement 3 - No. Locks only apply to control plane Azure operations and not to data plane operations. Deleting a blob with AzCopy and an account key is a data plane request to the storage service endpoint, so the lock does not block it - Microsoft states that a read-only lock or cannot-delete lock on a storage account doesn't protect the data in a blob, queue, table, or file. Note the contrast: the same lock would block a control plane delete such as the File Shares - Delete ARM operation.
tags: resource locks,lock inheritance,management groups,data plane,storage account

sotto_argomento: Apply and manage tags on resources
domanda:
You use the Azure portal to assign the built-in policy definition named 'Inherit a tag from the resource group if missing' at the scope of a subscription. You configure the tag name Department and select a system-assigned managed identity for the assignment. The subscription already contains hundreds of resources, many of which have no Department tag. Evaluate each of the following statements and indicate whether it is true.

1. The resources that already exist and are missing the Department tag are tagged automatically at the end of the next policy evaluation cycle.
2. If a new resource is created with a Department tag whose value differs from the value on its parent resource group, the policy replaces the resource's value with the resource group's value.
3. Because you created the assignment in the Azure portal, Azure Policy grants the system-assigned managed identity the roles that are listed in the definition's roleDefinitionIds property.
opzione_a: The resources that already exist and are missing the Department tag are tagged automatically at the end of the next policy evaluation cycle.
opzione_b: If a new resource is created with a Department tag whose value differs from the value on its parent resource group, the policy replaces the resource's value with the resource group's value.
opzione_c: Because you created the assignment in the Azure portal, Azure Policy grants the system-assigned managed identity the roles that are listed in the definition's roleDefinitionIds property.
spiegazione: Statement 1 - No. This is the most commonly missed behaviour of the modify effect. When a policy definition using the modify effect is run as part of an evaluation cycle, it doesn't make changes to resources that already exist; instead, it marks any resource that meets the if condition as non-compliant so it can be remediated through a remediation task. Modify evaluates before the request is processed by a resource provider, so it only acts on creation or update requests. You must create a remediation task to tag the existing resources. Statement 2 - No. The chosen definition is the 'if missing' variant, which Microsoft describes as: 'Adds the specified tag with its value from the parent resource group when any resource missing this tag is created or updated... If the tag exists with a different value it will not be changed.' It uses the Add operation, not addOrReplace. To overwrite a differing value you would assign 'Inherit a tag from the resource group' instead. Statement 3 - Yes. Policy assignments with the modify effect require a managed identity to do remediation. When you use the portal, Azure Policy automatically grants the managed identity the listed roles once assignment starts; the roles must be granted manually only when you create the assignment with an SDK, PowerShell, or the CLI. Note that if roleDefinitionIds are later edited in the definition, the new permissions must be granted manually even in the portal.
tags: tags,azure policy,modify effect,inherit a tag,remediation task,managed identity
